title: Kepler's Laws of Planetary Motion
short_intro: Kepler's laws are three empirical laws describing the kinematic properties of planetary motion around the Sun, formulated by Johannes Kepler using Tycho Brahe's astronomical data. They form the foundational bridge between observational astronomy and Newtonian mechanics.

exam_scope.tgt_core: Qualitative statements of the three laws, calculation of time periods using Kepler's Third Law (T² is proportional to r³), identification of orbital parameters like semi-major axis, and conservation of angular momentum in central orbits.
exam_scope.pgt_extension: Rigorous derivation of Kepler's Second Law as a consequence of conservation of angular momentum, derivation of Kepler's Third Law for circular and elliptical orbits using Newton's law of gravitation, total energy of an orbiting body, and effective potential energy.

concept_notes.heading: Kepler's First Law (Law of Orbits)
bullets: All planets move in elliptical orbits with the Sun located at one of the two foci.
The eccentricity (e) of an ellipse lies between 0 and 1 (0 < e < 1). For a circle, e = 0.
The closest point of approach to the Sun is the perihelion, and the farthest point is the aphelion.

concept_notes.heading: Kepler's Second Law (Law of Areas)
bullets: A line segment joining a planet and the Sun sweeps out equal areas in equal intervals of time.
This law is a direct consequence of the conservation of angular momentum, as the gravitational force is a central force exerting zero torque.
Planets move fastest at the perihelion and slowest at the aphelion.

concept_notes.heading: Kepler's Third Law (Law of Periods)
bullets: The square of the time period of revolution of a planet is directly proportional to the cube of the semi-major axis of its elliptical orbit.
Expressed mathematically as T² = k r³, where k depends only on the mass of the central body (the Sun).
It establishes that outer planets take significantly longer to complete one orbit around the Sun.

concept_notes.heading: Connection to Central Forces and Newtonian Mechanics
bullets: Newton demonstrated that Kepler's laws imply an inverse-square central gravitational force F = -GMm/r² r̂.
The motion occurs entirely in a plane due to zero net external torque acting about the Sun.
The total mechanical energy of a bound planetary orbit is negative (E < 0).

derivations.title: Derivation of Kepler's Second Law from Conservation of Angular Momentum
derivations.conditions: Central force field acting on a planet of mass m
steps: The areal velocity of a planet vectorially is given by dA/dt =  rac{1}{2} |r 	imes v|.
Substitute linear momentum p = mv into the cross product to get dA/dt =  rac{1}{2m} |r 	imes p|.
Since r 	imes p is the angular momentum L, dA/dt =  rac{L}{2m}.
Because gravitational force is a central force, torque τ =  rac{dL}{dt} = 0, meaning L is constant.
Therefore, the areal velocity  rac{dA}{dt} is constant, proving Kepler's Second Law.

derivations.title: Derivation of Kepler's Third Law for Circular Orbits
derivations.conditions: Planet of mass m moving in a circular orbit of radius r around a Sun of mass M
steps: Equate the gravitational force to the required centripetal force: \frac{GMm}{r^2} = \frac{mv^2}{r}.
Express velocity v in terms of distance r and time period T as v = \frac{2\pi r}{T}.
Substitute the expression for v into the force balance equation: \frac{GM}{r^2} = \frac{1}{r} \left(\frac{2\pi r}{T}\right)^2.
Rearrange to solve for T^2: T^2 = \left(\frac{4\pi^2}{GM}\right) r^3.

formula_sheet.name: Kepler's Third Law
formula_sheet.variables: T = Time period, G = Gravitational constant, M = Mass of central body, r = Semi-major axis
formula_sheet.units: T in s, r in m, M in kg

formula_sheet.name: Areal Velocity
formula_sheet.variables: A = Area swept, t = Time, L = Angular momentum, m = Mass of planet
formula_sheet.conditions: Valid for any central force motion

formula_sheet.name: Perihelion and Aphelion Distances
formula_sheet.equation_html: r_p = a(1 - e), \quad r_a = a(1 + e)
formula_sheet.variables: a = Semi-major axis, e = Eccentricity, r_p = Perihelion distance, r_a = Aphelion distance

formula_sheet.name: Conservation of Angular Momentum at Perihelion and Aphelion
formula_sheet.equation_html: m r_p v_p = m r_a v_a
formula_sheet.variables: r_p, r_a = Distances, v_p, v_a = Velocities at perihelion and aphelion
formula_sheet.conditions: Motion in a plane under central force

formula_sheet.name: Orbital Velocity in Elliptical Orbit
formula_sheet.variables: v = Orbital velocity, r = Instantaneous distance, a = Semi-major axis

formula_sheet.name: Total Mechanical Energy of Orbiting Planet
formula_sheet.variables: E = Total energy, G = Gravitational constant, M, m = Masses, a = Semi-major axis
formula_sheet.conditions: Gravitational potential energy reference at infinity

formula_sheet.name: Gravitational Force Law from Kepler's Laws
formula_sheet.variables: F = Force vector, r = Radius vector magnitude, r̂ = Unit vector

formula_sheet.conditions: Applicable to all planets orbiting the Sun

graphs_and_experiments.title: Elliptical Orbit and Equal Areas in Equal Times
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: An ellipse with the Sun at one focus F. Draw sectors S1 and S2 swept out by the planet in equal time intervals Δt, showing equal areas A1 = A2.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: The arc length covered near perihelion is longer than near aphelion, demonstrating that the linear speed of the planet varies along the orbit.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Tested conceptually in TGT to check understanding of planetary speed variation and areal velocity.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Logarithmic Plot of Kepler's Third Law (log T vs log r)
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A straight line plot on a log-log scale with log(T) on the y-axis and log(r) on the x-axis.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: The slope of the straight line is exactly 3/2, confirming the relationship T &proportional; r^(3/2).
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Tested in PGT to interpret experimental power-law relations from graphical data.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Effective Potential and Total Energy Graph
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A plot of effective potential energy U_eff(r) = \frac{L^2}{2mr^2} - \frac{GMm}{r} versus radial distance r.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Shows a deep potential well with a minimum corresponding to stable circular orbits, and total energy E crossing the curve at two turning points (perihelion and aphelion).
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Used in PGT to analyze bound states, turning points, and stability of orbits.

solved_numericals.question: If the distance of a planet from the Sun becomes half of its present distance, what will be the new time period of revolution?
solution_steps: State Kepler's Third Law: T² is proportional to r³.
Set up the ratio: (T_2 / T_1)² = (r_2 / r_1)³.
Substitute r_2 = r_1 / 2 into the equation: (T_2 / T_1)² = (1 / 2)³ = 1 / 8.
Take the square root on both sides: T_2 / T_1 = \sqrt{1 / 8} = \frac{1}{2\sqrt{2}}.
Write the final answer in terms of T_1: T_2 = \frac{T_1}{2\sqrt{2}}.

solved_numericals.question: A satellite orbits a planet of mass M in an elliptical orbit. Its closest distance is r_1 and farthest distance is r_2. Find the ratio of its speeds at these two extreme positions (v_1 / v_2).
solution_steps: Apply the principle of conservation of angular momentum about the center of force (focus): m r_1 v_1 = m r_2 v_2.
Cancel mass m from both sides: r_1 v_1 = r_2 v_2.
Rearrange to find the ratio of velocities v_1 / v_2: \frac{v_1}{v_2} = \frac{r_2}{r_1}.
Interpret the physical result: speed is inversely proportional to distance from the center.

solved_numericals.question: Calculate the total mechanical energy of an artificial satellite of mass 200 kg orbiting the Earth (mass M = 6 \times 10^{24} kg, radius R = 6400 km) in a circular orbit at a height equal to the Earth's radius.
solution_steps: Identify the orbital radius r = R + h = R + R = 2R = 2 \times 6.4 \times 10^6 m = 1.28 \times 10^7 m.
State the total energy formula for a circular orbit: E = -\frac{GMm}{2r}.
Substitute the given values (G = 6.67 \times 10^{-11} N m^2/kg^2, M = 6 \times 10^{24} kg, m = 200 kg):
Calculate final numerical value: E = -3.126 \times 10^9 J.

assumptions_and_limitations: Kepler's laws assume a two-body system (Sun and a single planet) and neglect gravitational perturbations caused by other planets.
Planets are treated as point masses or spherically symmetric bodies, ignoring oblateness and non-uniform density distributions.
Relativistic corrections (such as perihelion precession explained by General Relativity) are ignored in classical Keplerian motion.

common_misconceptions.wrong: The Sun is located at the center of the elliptical orbit.
common_misconceptions.correct: The Sun is located at one of the two foci of the ellipse, not the geometric center.
common_misconceptions.why: An ellipse has two foci; the geometric center is equidistant from the vertices, whereas the Sun occupies only one focus point.

common_misconceptions.wrong: Kepler's laws apply only to planets orbiting the Sun.
common_misconceptions.correct: Kepler's laws apply to any system bound by an inverse-square central force, including satellites around Earth and binary star systems.
common_misconceptions.why: Newton generalized Kepler's third law to include the mass of both interacting bodies (M + m).

common_misconceptions.wrong: A planet moves with constant speed throughout its elliptical orbit.
common_misconceptions.correct: A planet's speed continuously changes, being maximum at perihelion and minimum at aphelion.
common_misconceptions.why: Conservation of angular momentum requires that as the radius vector changes, the linear speed must change inversely to keep areal velocity constant.

quick_revision: Kepler's 1st Law: Orbits are ellipses with the Sun at one focus.
Kepler's 2nd Law: Areal velocity (dA/dt = L/2m) is constant, reflecting conservation of angular momentum.
Kepler's 3rd Law: T² is proportional to r³.
Gravitational force is an inverse-square central force producing zero net torque.
